5.2 — The Door: Opening It with Events

You have an axe, and the cave door does not care — yet. Today you close the last gap: press E near a lever, the lever fires a UnityEvent, and the door opens without the lever ever knowing what a door is. That gap between cause and effect is called abstraction, and it is the most exam-relevant idea in this whole project.

Read the Code That Ships ~10 min

This is the one script in Assets/Scripts/ that is not an empty shell. Open Assets/Scripts/Lever.cs and read the whole thing — it is short. Here is the part that matters, quoted: 

[SerializeField] private UnityEvent onLeverOn;
[SerializeField] private UnityEvent onLeverOff;
// ... later, inside Interact():
onLeverOn.Invoke();

Notice what is missing: the word "door" appears nowhere in that file. The lever has no idea what it is switching on. It flips a sprite, and it fires an event — and who is listening is somebody else's business entirely.

Now open the Overworld scene, select the Switch object, and look at its Inspector. You will see the two UnityEvent fields, both currently empty. The lever is shouting into a room with nobody in it. Wiring those up is Step 2 below — and it involves no code at all.

Socratic: Where does the game's knowledge live?

  1. The lever opens a door it has never met. Which window do you open to teach it about the door — and what does your answer say about where the game's rules actually live?
  2. If the lever had been written the obvious way — holding a reference to the door and calling door.Open() directly — what would you have to change to make a second lever open a second door? What does the event version cost instead?
  3. The exam calls a procedure that calls other procedures without knowing their names abstraction. Write down what the lever would have needed to know without UnityEvent, and what complexity the event removes.
  4. Could the lever use an event to trigger something that has nothing to do with doors? Give an example, and say why that is a strength rather than a bug.
Build Lab: The interaction ~25 min

The lever works. What does not exist yet is any way for the player to reach it. Press E right now and nothing happens, because nothing in PlayerController listens for it.

Socratic: Three ways to decide "am I near a lever?"

You have solved this shape of problem twice already, but never for an interaction. Compare:

ApproachHow it worksWhat it costs
Search and measure On the key press, find every lever in the scene, measure the distance to each, and interact with the ones close enough. A scene-wide search and a distance check for each lever. Simple to reason about, but it scales badly and it re-does work the physics engine could have done for you.
A trigger zone around the lever Give the lever a large trigger collider. Track when the player enters and leaves it, and remember the lever you are currently standing in. You must add a component and manage the "which one am I inside" state yourself. But the physics engine does the proximity test for free, every frame.
Look forward from the player On the key press, cast a short ray in the direction the player faces to find what is in front of them. Requires the player to face the lever, and to know which way they face. More precise, more situational.
  1. Which approach did you use for turret detection in 3.1? Which of these three is the closest cousin to it, and why is the analogy not perfect?
  2. There is exactly one Switch in the Overworld today. Which approach is over-engineered for one lever, and which one would you regret not choosing if the cave had twelve?
  3. Whichever you pick, what does "close enough" mean numerically — and where should that number live so a designer can change it?
  4. Which key event should trigger the interaction: the one that fires every frame the key is held, or the one that fires once on press? What would happen with the wrong choice?
Architectural specification: the interaction.
  • Which callback in PlayerController should hold this, and which input method detects a single key press rather than a held key?
  • What method on the lever do you need to call? Read Lever.cs and find its public method — what is it called, and why must it be public for you to reach it?
  • How do you get a reference to the Lever component itself rather than to the GameObject? Which method does that?
  • What is your proximity test, and what will you compare against?
  • What happens if your search finds nothing? Write the guard before you need it.

Step 2 — wire the door, with no code at all. There is no door object in this scene yet, so build one: a new sprite (or a wall segment) placed over the cave mouth. Now select the Switch and find On Lever On in the Inspector. Click the plus to add a listener, drag your door into the slot, and choose what to call — GameObject → SetActive(false) is the simplest honest door.

Press Play, walk to the lever, press E. The door obeys. You just changed the game's rules from the Inspector, with zero lines of code.

Step 3 — the design question. The door should only open for someone holding the axe. Read Lever.cs again: does it check anything about the axe? No — the lever checks nothing at all. So where should that check live: in the lever, on the door, or in the player? Write your answer down and defend it. There is a strong argument for each, and the next lesson takes the door off its hinges anyway.

Bug Hunt: The event that wouldn't

  1. If you chose search-and-measure, remove the distance check and press E from across the map. What did that check protect you from?
  2. Wire the door's SetActive(false) into On Lever Off instead of On. Now what is the exact key-press sequence to get through? Is that a puzzle or a bug?
  3. Clear the lever's onSprite field so it has no sprite to swap to. Does the event still fire? Which of the two is decoration, and which is the machinery?
  4. Add a second Switch and stand between them so both are in range. Press E once. What happened — and should one keypress ever flip two switches? Which of the three approaches would prevent it?
  5. Give the lever a trigger zone (if you chose that approach) and then walk away without pressing E. Does the lever still think you are nearby? What state are you failing to clear?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Event design

  1. Wire the lever to two listeners at once: open the door and play a sound or a second animation. Does the lever need to know there are two? Why is "whoever wants to know, listens" the direction that scales?
  2. Make a false wall that opens a secret passage instead of the cave. How much code did that cost you — and what does that number tell you about the value of the event pattern?
  3. Make the lever refuse to work unless the player holds the axe. Which script gains a conditional — and can you do it with zero changes to Lever.cs? (Hint: think about who is allowed to be a listener.)
  4. The lever is shouting into an empty room until someone subscribes. What happens if you wire a listener, then delete the object it points at? What does Unity show you in the Inspector?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain a UnityEvent as cause-and-effect with a deliberate gap: the lever never names the door
  • Wire a listener in the Inspector and change the game's rules with no code
  • Compare three ways to detect "the player is near a lever", and defend yours
  • Explain why Interact() must be public
  • Argue where an item-gate check belongs, and name the cost of each placement
  • Commit and push
